title: Olympic National Park Travel Guide

hero.alt: Olympic National Park mountains, temperate rain forest, and Pacific coast
hero.headline: Olympic National Park Travel Guide
hero.subheadline: Plan Olympic around Hurricane Ridge, the Hoh and Quinault rain forests, Lake Crescent, Sol Duc, wild Pacific beaches, and the Elwha River restoration across one unusually diverse national park.

overview: Olympic National Park wraps around the heart of Washington's Olympic Peninsula and protects three strikingly different environments: glacier-cut mountains, old-growth temperate rain forests, and more than 70 miles of wild Pacific coastline. No road crosses the park's mountainous center, so places that look close on a map can require long drives around the peninsula.

A strong first visit is built as a circuit. Use Port Angeles for Hurricane Ridge and Lake Crescent, spend a separate block in the Hoh or Quinault rain forest, and give the coast its own tide-aware day around Rialto, Ruby, or Kalaloch. The park is also inseparable from the Indigenous nations of the Olympic Peninsula and from the landmark restoration of the Elwha River.

highlights.title: Mountains to ocean
highlights.description: Move from alpine ridges and glaciated peaks to giant forests and surf-beaten beaches within one protected landscape.

highlights.title: Temperate rain forest
highlights.description: Walk beneath moss-draped Sitka spruce, western hemlock, Douglas-fir, and bigleaf maple in some of North America's wettest forests.

highlights.title: Wild Pacific coast
highlights.description: Explore sea stacks, tide pools, driftwood beaches, and headlands while planning carefully around tides and surf.

highlights.title: Living cultural landscape
highlights.description: Recognize the enduring connections of Olympic Peninsula Tribes and the modern ecological restoration of the Elwha watershed.

thingsToDo.title: Climb to Hurricane Ridge for Olympic Mountain views
thingsToDo.description: Hurricane Ridge is the park's easiest high-elevation access from Port Angeles, rising from coastal lowlands into subalpine meadows and broad views of the Olympic Mountains. Short walks and longer ridge trails reveal how quickly elevation changes vegetation and weather. Clear days can expose a rugged skyline of peaks and glacial valleys, while fog, wind, snow, or clouds can erase the view within minutes. The access road is steep and seasonal conditions can affect it outside midsummer. Check current NPS road and facility status before driving, and remember that wildlife and fragile meadow plants need space even when trails begin beside pavement.

thingsToDo.title: Walk the Hoh Rain Forest
thingsToDo.description: The Hoh is one of the best-known temperate rain forests in the United States, fed by moisture moving inland from the Pacific and rising against the Olympic Mountains. The Hall of Mosses and Spruce Nature Trail provide short introductions to giant trees, nurse logs, ferns, hanging mosses, and a forest floor built from centuries of decay and regrowth. Longer trails follow the Hoh River toward the park's mountainous interior. Summer parking can fill and entrance lines can become long, so arrive early. Rain is not a failure here; precipitation is one of the ecological forces that created the forest visitors came to see.

thingsToDo.title: Explore Lake Crescent and Marymere Falls
thingsToDo.description: Lake Crescent occupies a deep glacial basin west of Port Angeles and reaches depths of more than 600 feet. Its clear blue water is surrounded by steep forested mountains, making it a strong base for paddling, shoreline walking, and hiking when conditions allow. The short Marymere Falls trail passes through old forest to a 90-foot waterfall, while Mount Storm King is a much steeper and more demanding climb above the lake. Historic Lake Crescent Lodge adds early park-tourism context. Water remains cold even in warm weather, so boating and swimming deserve the same caution as other mountain lakes.

thingsToDo.title: Visit Sol Duc Valley and Sol Duc Falls
thingsToDo.description: Sol Duc Valley combines old-growth forest, river habitat, hot-spring history, and one of Olympic's most photogenic waterfalls. A forest trail reaches Sol Duc Falls, where the river divides into channels and drops through a narrow rocky gorge. The valley also provides trail access toward high-country routes and the Seven Lakes Basin. Salmon returning through the watershed add another ecological story. Road and resort operations are seasonal, and winter storms can close access. Pair Sol Duc with Lake Crescent rather than attempting to cross the peninsula repeatedly in one day.

thingsToDo.title: Walk Rialto Beach and the Mora coast
thingsToDo.description: Rialto Beach presents Olympic's Pacific coast in its rawest form: surf, dark cobbles, giant driftwood, offshore sea stacks, and forest reaching close to the beach. Strong hikers often continue north toward Hole-in-the-Wall when tides permit. Tide tables are essential because headlands and narrow beach sections can become dangerous or impassable as water rises. Large drift logs can also move suddenly in surf. Keep substantial distance from wildlife and never turn your back on the ocean. The coast is part of a broader Indigenous cultural landscape connected to Tribal communities whose relationships with these shores long predate national-park boundaries.

thingsToDo.title: See Ruby Beach and the Kalaloch coast
thingsToDo.description: Ruby Beach and nearby Kalaloch offer accessible views of Olympic's southern Pacific shoreline, with sea stacks, tide pools, driftwood, and broad beaches. Low tide reveals intertidal communities that disappear beneath the water hours later, so plan around a current tide table rather than a clock-only itinerary. Tide pools contain living animals easily damaged by careless feet or hands. Kalaloch's coastal forest and bluffs also demonstrate active shoreline erosion; trees can be undermined as storms and waves remove sediment. These beaches work well as a separate coastal day paired with the Hoh or Quinault side of the peninsula.

thingsToDo.title: See the Elwha River restoration landscape
thingsToDo.description: The Elwha River became the site of one of the world's largest dam-removal and ecosystem-restoration projects. Elwha Dam and Glines Canyon Dam, built in the early 20th century without fish passage, blocked salmon from much of the watershed. Their removal between 2011 and 2014 reopened more than 70 miles of habitat and released sediment that began rebuilding downstream river and coastal systems. The project also carries deep cultural importance for the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe. Roads and trails in the Elwha area can be affected by washouts and flood damage, so check current access before visiting.

thingsToDo.title: Explore Quinault Rain Forest and Lake Quinault
thingsToDo.description: The Quinault side of the peninsula offers another major temperate-rain-forest experience, with enormous conifers, fern-filled forest, waterfalls, and Lake Quinault at the edge of national park and national forest lands. Roads and trails form a useful southern gateway into the park, while the broader Quinault landscape is culturally connected to the Quinault Indian Nation. Pay attention to land-management boundaries because not every road, forest tract, or lakeshore facility is administered by the National Park Service. A slower drive and short walks here provide a strong alternative to treating the Hoh as Olympic's only rain forest.

bestTimeToVisit.title: Olympic's coast, rain forests, and mountains run on different seasons
bullets: Summer generally provides the broadest mountain-road and trail access, but it is also the busiest period at Hurricane Ridge, Hoh, and major beaches.
Spring brings waterfalls, river flow, and green forests while snow can remain in the high country.
Fall is quieter and wet weather becomes more frequent, especially on the west side of the peninsula.
Winter storms transform the coast and rain forests while snow limits mountain access; road closures and fallen trees are common planning factors.

travelTips: Do not plan Olympic as though a road crosses the center; driving times around the peninsula are substantial.
Carry a current tide table for coastal hikes and know which headlands become impassable at high tide.
Check road conditions before every mountain or remote-valley drive because washouts, snow, and storms can change access.
Keep food secured from wildlife and maintain required distances from elk, bears, mountain goats, and marine animals.
Respect Tribal lands and boundaries around the peninsula; national park, reservation, national forest, and private lands are distinct jurisdictions.

faq.q: How many days should I spend in Olympic National Park?
faq.a: Three to four days is a useful minimum for a first visit because the mountains, rain forests, and coast are separated by long drives. Five days gives much better flexibility for hiking and weather.

faq.q: Can I drive through the center of Olympic National Park?
faq.a: No. The mountainous core has no through-road. Visitor roads approach from the perimeter, so travel between Hurricane Ridge, the Hoh, and the Pacific coast goes around the park.

faq.q: Which rain forest should I visit?
faq.a: The Hoh is the best-known and has classic short trails, while Quinault offers a broader lake-and-forest landscape and can fit naturally into a south-side peninsula loop. Both reward wet-weather visits.

faq.q: Why is the Elwha River important?
faq.a: Removal of two large dams from 2011 to 2014 reopened extensive salmon habitat and triggered major river and coastal restoration. The watershed is also culturally important to the Lower Elwha Klallam Tribe.

faq.q: What makes Olympic unusual among national parks?
faq.a: One park protects high mountains, temperate rain forest, major river systems, and a long undeveloped Pacific coastline, with enormous ecological change over relatively short straight-line distances.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Olympic National Park is a protected peninsula landscape, not a city. Its disconnected road approaches reflect a mountainous wilderness core surrounded by rain forests, lakes, river valleys, and Pacific coastline.

sections.heading: Geography & geology
paragraphs: The Olympic Mountains were built from marine rocks uplifted as tectonic plates converged along the Pacific margin. Glaciers carved mountain valleys and lake basins, while Pacific storms create extreme precipitation gradients between the wet western rain forests and drier northeastern peninsula.

sections.heading: Indigenous and park history
paragraphs: Eight contemporary Tribal nations maintain relationships with the Olympic Peninsula and park landscape, including Makah, Quileute, Hoh, Quinault, Skokomish, Port Gamble S'Klallam, Jamestown S'Klallam, and Lower Elwha Klallam communities. Federal forest protection began in the 1890s, and Olympic became a national park in 1938.

sections.heading: Outdoor & seasonal highlights
paragraphs: Hiking, backpacking, paddling, tide-pool exploration, wildlife observation, fishing under current regulations, snow travel, and scenic driving span environments whose weather can differ dramatically on the same day.

sections.heading: Getting around
paragraphs: Highway 101 circles much of the peninsula and feeds separate park roads into Hurricane Ridge, Lake Crescent and Sol Duc, the Hoh, Quinault, and coastal areas. Build a loop itinerary rather than repeatedly returning to one base.
